newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr fights profit-taking tide.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr fights profit-taking tide.

text.p: The Australian dollar became a victim of its own success Thursday as recent rich gains attracted a rush of profit-taking.

Dealers said a failure to stay abreast of the US$0.7910 barrier looked to some like confirmation of a medium term top. The resultant chart-driven selling cleaved 3/4 cent off its value and seemed set to bust US$0.7820 support this morning.

However, the currency was cupped by offshore demand, with U.S. momentum funds rumoured buyers and reports of good Japanese interest on the bid side around 95.00 yen. The net result was to leave the uptrend intact, if a little frayed at the edges.
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the dollar had drooped to US$0.7845/50 from US$0.7870/75 late Wednesday and a US$0.7912 peak Tuesday.

That was still a decent distance from the key US$0.7820 chart level, a breach of which would have brought a premature conclusion to its month old rally and threaten a return to US$0.7740 at least or even the one-year low of US$0.7550 hit on February 12.

On the other hand the recapture of US$0.7876 -- its 200-day moving average -- would indicate the correction was past and a re-test of US$0.7910 likely next week. In such a case the bull targets would be US$0.7960 followed by a lofty US$0.8050.
On the crosses the dollar faded as far as 94.86 yen at one stage after Japan reported a surprise jump in its current account surplus to 150.7 billion yen in January, the first rise for 17 months.
This stirred concerns about renewed U.S./Japanese trade tensions and a U.S. official did say the administration would be concerned if the rise was the start of an upward trend.

That knocked the U.S. currency below 121.00 but it found good demand there and rallied to 122.70/75. The local dollar also attracted Japanese demand and recovered to 95.51/61 yen, but that was still off on Wednesday's late 95.77/87.
It also ran into profit taking on the mark, Swiss franc and NZ$ which shaved 0.2 point off its trade weighted index to 60.2.

Again, the dollar was well off early trough and dealers could see little reason to expect a sustained reversal in its long uptrend with interest rates in Japan and Europe at or near record lows and domestic policy on hold.

But there was a risk U.S. rates could be rising soon, thus paring the A$'s already slender yield premium over the US$. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan hinted as much last week and did nothing to dispell the speculation in a finely balanced assessment of the economy to the House banking committee today.
Greenspan said the economy was running close to capacity constraints and the Fed had to act pre-emptively to constrain inflation even before concrete signs of price pressures emerged.

However, he added the economy was not overheating and neither was inflation accelerating, and noted the Fed had left rates unchanged in the second half of 1996 even though the economy had been close to its capacity limits.

The balance left analysts neatly divided with some confidently expecting a 0.25 point hike in the 5.25 percent Fed funds rate at its next policy meeting on March 25, and others predicting a steady policy for months yet.

Today's domestic data on foreign debt showed Australia moved deeper into the red in the December quarter than anyone had thought. Net debt jumped to A$202.37 billion from an upwardly revised A$196.04 billion in Q3 while the debt to GDP ratio rose to 40.1 percent, its first venture above 40.0 in three years.
Most of the increase was in public sector debt which did not fit well with government protestations it had tightened fiscal policy enough to reduce its demands on domestic savings.
In any case, analysts said the data had no relevance for monetary policy and so were studiously ignored by markets.
